   Lawsuits are time-consuming and expensive, so many jurisdictions encourage resolving neighbor disputes out of court first. Send a formal, dated cease-and-desist letter (you can draft this with initial legal input) to your neighbor outlining the issues and demanding they stop the problematic behavior. You may also pursue mediation, a voluntary process where a neutral third party helps you and your neighbor reach a mutually acceptable agreement—many local governments offer low-cost or free mediation services for neighborhood conflicts.
3. Consult a local property law attorney
   Reach out to a licensed attorney in your area who specializes in property or civil litigation. They can confirm if your claims meet the legal definitions of nuisance (which typically requires the activity to unreasonably and substantially interfere with your use and enjoyment of your property) and trespass (which often involves unauthorised physical entry onto your land or a failure to remove property/objects they placed there without permission). They can also advise you on the statute of limitations for filing your claim, which varies by location, and help you navigate court procedures if mediation fails.
4. Evaluate court options
   If out-of-court resolution is impossible, your attorney can help you choose the right court to file your claim. For minor damages, small claims court may be a more accessible, low-cost option (each jurisdiction sets a maximum dollar limit for small claims). For larger damages or to seek a permanent injunction (a court order forcing your neighbor to stop the problematic behavior), you may need to file in a higher civil court.

Always rely on your attorney’s guidance to ensure you follow all local legal rules and protect your rights properly.

Your strategy needs to be low-lift, low-minimum-investment, and aligned with your transient, often tight-budget lifestyle. Here’s a flexible, foundational framework:
1. Pre-investment foundation (non-negotiable first steps)
   - Catalog your full financial picture: List all steady income (stipends, side hustles), fixed expenses, and any high-interest debt (credit cards, private student loans with >7% interest). For high-interest debt, eliminating this first beats most investment returns, as you’ll save more on interest than you’d earn from market investments.
   - Build a mini emergency fund first: Stash $1,000–$2,000 in a high-yield savings account (HYSA) to cover unexpected costs (textbook replacements, laptop repairs) so you don’t dip into investments. Once high-interest debt is paid off, expand this to 3–6 months of essential expenses.
   - Prioritize "human capital investments" first: For grad students, this is one of the highest-return moves. Allocate a small portion of your budget to certifications, conference travel, or side projects that boost your post-grad earning potential—higher lifetime income will accelerate your path to financial independence far more than small early investment gains.
2. Accessible, low-stakes investment steps for your current income level
   - Open a tax-advantaged account aligned with your low tax bracket: If you’re a U.S. resident with earned income (stipends/side income that qualifies as earned), a Roth IRA is ideal. You pay minimal taxes on contributions now (since you’re in a low tax bracket), and all withdrawals in retirement are tax-free. Many brokers allow Roth IRAs with $0 minimum opening deposits, so you can contribute $25–$50/month consistently.
   - Choose low-cost, diversified investments: Stick to broad-market index funds or ETFs (e.g., S&P 500 total stock market, total international stock market funds) with expense ratios under 0.10%. These spread your risk across thousands of companies, avoiding the volatility of picking individual stocks. For a hands-off option, target-date funds automatically rebalance to lower risk as you near retirement, though check their fees first.
   - Automate small contributions: Set up auto-transfers of $20–$50/month from your checking account to your investment account immediately after you get your stipend. Consistency matters more than large sums here—this habit will scale easily when you get a higher post-grad salary.
3. Adjust as your circumstances change post-grad
   - Once you secure a full-time job, increase your investment contributions to 15–20% of your income (the standard threshold to reach financial independence in 30–40 years). If your employer offers a 401(k) match, contribute enough to claim the full match first—it’s free money that accelerates your goals.
   - Reassess your student loan strategy: If you have low-interest federal student loans (<5%), you can continue investing while making standard payments, but if rates are higher, accelerate loan paydown alongside investments to reduce long-term interest costs.
4. Key pitfalls to avoid
   - Skip speculative assets (meme stocks, crypto, risky startup investments) unless you can afford to lose every dollar you put in—your limited grad student budget can’t absorb major losses.
   - Don’t cash out investments early if you switch jobs or face a temporary cash crunch; early Roth IRA withdrawals (before 59.5) can trigger penalties, and you’ll lose out on compound growth.
